summary.text: 岁 is the standardized simplified form of 歲, commonly meaning “year” and also “age.” In a later seal-script analysis, 歲 was parsed as 步 plus phonetic 戌; that lexicographic account does not establish the early graph’s origin.

formation.text: The early formation of 歲 is disputed. Some early forms are analyzed as 步, contributing movement, with 戉 as a proposed sound element; another account proposes that the graph was borrowed from 戉 and later differentiated. The later seal-script form was analyzed as 步 with phonetic 戌. These analyses do not establish one original construction, and the visible parts of 岁 do not prove its origin.

components.text: In the seal-script analysis of 歲, 步 contributes the idea of walking or movement. This is a later component analysis and does not show that every early form contained 步.

In the seal-script analysis of 歲, 戌 is identified as the phonetic element. This is a transmitted lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of the early graph’s construction or a historical sound match.

sound_limitation.text: The cited seal-script analysis identifies 戌 as phonetic, but the supplied reading comparison is modern and does not independently establish the historical phonetic relationship.

sound.text: Modern Mandarin readings are 戌 xū and 歲 suì; this pair records current readings and does not demonstrate their historical relation.

history.text: Paleographic accounts report oracle-bone forms used for “year” and also describe ritual interpretations; their graphic analyses differ. Later forms include analyses with 步, while the transmitted seal-script account parses 歲 as 步 plus 戌. The selected seal-script image is a modern vector redraw, not an ancient artifact.
岁 is reported as adapted from cursive 歲. The supplied evidence gives this proposed lineage without documenting its specific stages.

uncertainties.text: Early forms have been analyzed as movement plus a sound element, as a graph borrowed from 戉 and later differentiated, or in connection with ritual use. The depicted weapon’s ancient spoken name is not established, so its proposed sound connection to the year word cannot be fully tested.

senses.period: Oracle-bone period, as reported in supplied paleographic accounts; exact dates unresolved
senses.text: Paleographic accounts report oracle-bone use for “year,” but the evidence does not establish it as the earliest attested sense; ritual interpretations are also reported for this period.
A historical dictionary defines 歲 as Jupiter and describes its circuit through the lunar mansions over twelve months. This recorded sense does not establish the earliest spoken meaning.
“Age” is among the supplied glosses; its emergence and development from earlier uses are not established.

limitations.text: The reported oracle-bone use for “year” is not independently verified here against primary inscriptions; their full context and interpretation remain unchecked.
“Harvest” is listed as a gloss, but its chronology and connection to the other senses are not established.
A calendrical explanation links Jupiter’s roughly twelve-year circuit with “year,” but the evidence does not establish a historical transition between those senses.

overview.text: 岁 is the simplified form of 歲 and commonly means “year”; it is also used for “age.” The traditional graph has a later seal-script analysis involving movement and a sound element, but its early construction remains disputed.

components.text: In the seal-script analysis, 步 supplies the idea of walking or movement.
In that same analysis, 戌 is identified as the sound element; the modern readings xū and suì do not prove an ancient match.

relationships.text: The transmitted seal-script analysis parses 歲 as 从步戌聲; 步 is interpreted as contributing movement. This later analysis does not establish the component structure of every early form.

The transmitted seal-script analysis identifies 戌 as the phonetic element in 歲. Modern Mandarin 戌 xū and 歲 suì are available readings, but the comparison does not independently establish a historical sound match.
岁 is reported as the standardized simplified counterpart of 歲, adapted from its cursive form; this lineage is not independently confirmed by another supplied source.
